title: Matplotlib Canonical Cheatsheet
name: Matplotlib Cheatsheet
description: Canonical syntax recall for daily Matplotlib engineering work with production-ready, copy-paste snippets and compact lookup tables.

entries.title: Import pyplot and NumPy
entries.problem: Start a standard Matplotlib script with NumPy data.
entries.trigger: You need plotting plus array creation in one file.
entries.snippet:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
entries.minimal_notes: This is the default import pair for most scripts. Use `plt` for figure creation and `np` for data generation.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting `import numpy as np` before using sample data.

entries.title: Import Matplotlib core
entries.problem: Configure Matplotlib without pyplot.
entries.trigger: You need backend, rcParams, or non-plot utilities.
entries.snippet: import matplotlib as mpl
entries.minimal_notes: Use `matplotlib` for package-level settings and metadata. Keep plotting code in `pyplot` or OO objects.
entries.common_bug: Using `plt.rcParams` in code that should only depend on the core package.

entries.title: Use NumPy arrays with plotting
entries.problem: Plot computed arrays directly.
entries.trigger: Your data is already in NumPy form.
entries.snippet:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 200)
y = np.sin(x)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, y)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Matplotlib accepts NumPy arrays natively. Most scientific plots start this way.
entries.common_bug: Passing mismatched array lengths for `x` and `y`.

entries.title: Create a figure
entries.problem: Open a single canvas for manual Axes placement.
entries.trigger: You need explicit figure control before adding axes.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4), dpi=150, layout="constrained")
ax = fig.add_subplot(111)
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use `Figure` when you need direct control over size or canvas layout. Prefer `subplots()` when starting a normal multi-panel figure.
entries.common_bug: Creating a figure but never adding an Axes.

entries.title: Create subplots
entries.problem: Build a figure with one or more Axes at once.
entries.trigger: You need the standard OO workflow for one-panel or grid layouts.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4), layout="constrained")
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 5])
ax.set_title("Single panel")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: This is the most common production entry point. For multiple panels, `axs` is returned as an array.
entries.common_bug: Treating the returned Axes array like a single Axes object.

entries.title: Use subfigures
entries.problem: Split one figure into nested figure regions.
entries.trigger: You need independent layouts inside a larger page.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

fig = plt.figure(layout="constrained", figsize=(10, 4))
subfigs = fig.subfigures(1, 2, wspace=0.07)
x = np.linspace(0, 1, 50)

ax1 = subfigs[0].subplots()
ax1.plot(x, x**2)
ax1.set_title("Left")

ax2 = subfigs[1].subplots()
ax2.plot(x, np.sqrt(x))
ax2.set_title("Right")

plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use subfigures for complex dashboard-style layouts. They behave like nested figures.
entries.common_bug: Using subfigures when a simple subplot grid would be easier.

entries.title: Build a GridSpec layout
entries.problem: Place Axes with uneven row or column spans.
entries.trigger: You need a figure with asymmetric panel sizes.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig = plt.figure(layout="constrained", figsize=(8, 5))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 2)

ax1 = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, :])
ax2 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 0])
ax3 = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 1])

ax1.set_title("Top spans both columns")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `GridSpec` is the low-level layout tool for spans. Use it when `subplots()` is not enough.
entries.common_bug: Mixing `GridSpec` and manual `add_axes()` positions in the same layout.

entries.title: Build a mosaic layout
entries.problem: Name panels instead of indexing them manually.
entries.trigger: You want readable layout code for dashboards.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axd = plt.subplot_mosaic([["top", "top"], ["left", "right"]],
                              figsize=(8, 5), layout="constrained")
axd["top"].set_title("Top")
axd["left"].plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 2])
axd["right"].plot([1, 2, 3], [2, 1, 3])
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Mosaic layouts improve readability in multi-panel figures. They are ideal when panels have semantic names.
entries.common_bug: Reusing the same label unintentionally and overwriting a panel.

entries.title: Show a figure
entries.problem: Render the current figure in a script or notebook.
entries.trigger: You want the GUI or notebook backend to display output.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: In scripts, `show()` is the normal display step. In notebooks it may be implicit, but calling it is still safe.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting `show()` in script-based workflows.

entries.title: Close a figure
entries.problem: Free memory after generating plots.
entries.trigger: You create many figures in a loop or batch job.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
plt.close(fig)
entries.minimal_notes: Closing figures prevents memory growth in long-running jobs. Close figures you no longer need.
entries.common_bug: Leaving hundreds of figures open in automation or notebook loops.

entries.title: Create a line plot
entries.problem: Plot a continuous trend or series.
entries.trigger: You need the default chart for numeric sequences.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 200)
y = np.sin(x)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, y, label="sin(x)", linewidth=2)
ax.legend()
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `plot()` is the workhorse for line charts. Add labels early if a legend is needed.
entries.common_bug: Using `plot()` without specifying the x-values when order matters.

entries.title: Create a scatter plot
entries.problem: Show point-wise relationships or clusters.
entries.trigger: You need to visualize unconnected observations.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=200)
y = 0.5 * x + rng.normal(size=200)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(x, y, s=25, alpha=0.7)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use `scatter()` for point clouds and categorical jitter plots. Control size and alpha for dense data.
entries.common_bug: Passing huge markers without alpha, which hides structure.

entries.title: Create a bar chart
entries.problem: Compare discrete categories.
entries.trigger: You need vertical bars for counts, totals, or ranking.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

labels = ["A", "B", "C"]
values = [10, 14, 8]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(labels, values, color=["#4C78A8", "#F58518", "#54A24B"])
ax.set_ylabel("Value")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `bar()` is the default categorical comparison plot. Keep category labels short to avoid overlap.
entries.common_bug: Using numeric categories without setting tick labels clearly.

entries.title: Create a horizontal bar chart
entries.problem: Compare categories with long labels.
entries.trigger: Vertical labels would be hard to read.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

labels = ["Long label A", "Long label B", "Long label C"]
values = [10, 14, 8]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.barh(labels, values, color="#4C78A8")
ax.set_xlabel("Value")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `barh()` is better when labels are lengthy. It also works well for rankings.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to invert the y-axis when you want the highest value at the top.

entries.title: Create a histogram
entries.problem: Show the distribution of a numeric variable.
entries.trigger: You need frequency or density bins.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
data = rng.normal(size=1000)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(data, bins=30, edgecolor="white")
ax.set_xlabel("Value")
ax.set_ylabel("Count")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `hist()` is the standard distribution overview. Bin count changes the visual shape a lot.
entries.common_bug: Comparing histograms with different bin edges.

entries.title: Create a pie chart
entries.problem: Show part-to-whole proportions.
entries.trigger: You have a small number of categories that sum to a whole.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sizes = [40, 35, 25]
labels = ["A", "B", "C"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.pie(sizes, labels=labels, autopct="%1.1f%%", startangle=90)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use pie charts sparingly and only for simple proportions. Equal aspect keeps the circle round.
entries.common_bug: Omitting `ax.set_aspect("equal")` and getting an oval.

entries.title: Create a box plot
entries.problem: Compare distributions with quartiles and outliers.
entries.trigger: You need compact summary statistics across groups.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
data = [rng.normal(loc, 1, 200) for loc in [0, 1, 2]]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.boxplot(data, labels=["G1", "G2", "G3"])
ax.set_ylabel("Value")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `boxplot()` is useful for side-by-side group summaries. Use it when medians and spread matter.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to pass grouped sequences rather than one flattened array.

entries.title: Create a violin plot
entries.problem: Compare group distributions with shape information.
entries.trigger: You need more detail than a box plot provides.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
data = [rng.normal(loc, 1, 200) for loc in [0, 1, 2]]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.violinplot(data, showmeans=True, showmedians=True)
ax.set_xticks([1, 2, 3], ["G1", "G2", "G3"])
ax.set_ylabel("Value")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Violin plots show density shape as well as spread. They work well for distribution comparison across groups.
entries.common_bug: Not setting tick labels for the violin positions.

entries.title: Create a stem plot
entries.problem: Show discrete impulses or sample amplitudes.
entries.trigger: Your data is naturally sampled at individual points.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.arange(0, 10)
y = np.array([1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 2, 1, 3, 2, 4])

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.stem(x, y)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Stem plots emphasize each sample location. They are common in signal processing and integer-indexed data.
entries.common_bug: Using stem for dense continuous series where a line plot is clearer.

entries.title: Create a step plot
entries.problem: Show piecewise constant values or state changes.
entries.trigger: Your series changes at discrete boundaries.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
y = [1, 1, 3, 3, 2]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.step(x, y, where="mid")
ax.set_ylim(0, 4)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Step plots are ideal for sampled states and histogram-like trends. The `where` argument controls alignment.
entries.common_bug: Picking the wrong `where` value and shifting the visual transition.

entries.title: Create a stack plot
entries.problem: Show how multiple series add up over time.
entries.trigger: You need cumulative area comparison.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.arange(5)
y1 = np.array([1, 2, 1, 3, 2])
y2 = np.array([2, 1, 2, 1, 2])

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.stackplot(x, y1, y2, labels=["A", "B"])
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `stackplot()` is good for part-to-whole over an ordered x-axis. Keep the number of series small.
entries.common_bug: Stacking data that should actually be compared separately.

entries.title: Create an area fill plot
entries.problem: Shade the region under or between curves.
entries.trigger: You need emphasis on an interval or magnitude.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 200)
y = np.sin(x)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, y, color="black")
ax.fill_between(x, 0, y, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `fill_between()` is the common area chart primitive. It also works for confidence bands.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to plot the line, which makes the filled area harder to read.

entries.title: Create an error bar plot
entries.problem: Show measured values with uncertainty.
entries.trigger: You have standard deviations, confidence intervals, or measurement error.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.arange(5)
y = np.array([2.0, 2.5, 3.1, 2.8, 3.4])
err = np.array([0.2, 0.3, 0.1, 0.25, 0.15])

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.errorbar(x, y, yerr=err, fmt="o", capsize=4)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `errorbar()` is the standard uncertainty overlay. Use symmetric or asymmetric errors as needed.
entries.common_bug: Plotting error bars with the wrong units or scale.

entries.title: Create a hexbin plot
entries.problem: Visualize dense 2D point clouds.
entries.trigger: A scatter plot is too overplotted.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=5000)
y = x * 0.5 + rng.normal(size=5000)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
hb = ax.hexbin(x, y, gridsize=40, cmap="viridis")
fig.colorbar(hb, ax=ax)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Hexbin compresses dense scatter data into bins. Add a colorbar for counts or density.
entries.common_bug: Using hexbin on small datasets where scatter is clearer.

entries.title: Create contour lines
entries.problem: Show level curves of a 2D scalar field.
entries.trigger: You need isolines for scientific data.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 100)
y = np.linspace(-3, 3, 100)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
Z = np.sin(X) * np.cos(Y)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
cs = ax.contour(X, Y, Z, levels=10)
ax.clabel(cs, inline=True, fontsize=8)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `contour()` is the base isoline plot. Label contours only when the plot stays readable.
entries.common_bug: Passing 1D arrays instead of a meshgrid for gridded data.

entries.title: Create filled contours
entries.problem: Show continuous scalar fields with filled levels.
entries.trigger: You need a heatmap-like scientific surface.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 100)
y = np.linspace(-3, 3, 100)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
Z = np.sin(X) * np.cos(Y)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
cf = ax.contourf(X, Y, Z, levels=20, cmap="coolwarm")
fig.colorbar(cf, ax=ax)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `contourf()` is the filled version of contour plotting. Pair it with a colorbar.
entries.common_bug: Using too many levels and losing interpretability.

entries.title: Display an image
entries.problem: Render a matrix or raster array.
entries.trigger: You have image-like 2D data or pixel grids.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

img = np.random.default_rng(0).random((50, 50))

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
im = ax.imshow(img, cmap="viridis", origin="lower")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `imshow()` is the standard raster display API. Always check `origin` when orientation matters.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that image row 0 is often drawn at the top by default.

entries.title: Display a matrix as an image
entries.problem: Show array structure with row and column indexing.
entries.trigger: You want a matrix view rather than generic image semantics.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

mat = np.arange(16).reshape(4, 4)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
im = ax.matshow(mat, cmap="Blues")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `matshow()` is a convenience wrapper for matrix visualization. It is useful for small tables and matrices.
entries.common_bug: Using it for large arrays where labels become unreadable.

entries.title: Create a pseudocolor mesh
entries.problem: Visualize values on a rectangular grid.
entries.trigger: Your data is on cell corners or a grid surface.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0, 1, 40)
y = np.linspace(0, 1, 30)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
Z = np.sin(4 * np.pi * X) * np.cos(3 * np.pi * Y)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
pc = ax.pcolormesh(X, Y, Z, shading="auto", cmap="viridis")
fig.colorbar(pc, ax=ax)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `pcolormesh()` is often faster than contouring for gridded data. Use `shading="auto"` for modern defaults.
entries.common_bug: Dimension mismatch between grid coordinates and cell values.

entries.title: Create a quiver plot
entries.problem: Plot vector fields with arrows.
entries.trigger: You need direction and magnitude on a grid.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x, y = np.meshgrid(np.arange(0, 5), np.arange(0, 5))
u = np.cos(x)
v = np.sin(y)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.quiver(x, y, u, v)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `quiver()` is the standard arrow-field plot. Scale and normalization matter for readability.
entries.common_bug: Letting arrows overlap so densely that direction is unclear.

entries.title: Create a stream plot
entries.problem: Show flow lines for a vector field.
entries.trigger: You want continuous trajectories instead of arrows.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(-2, 2, 40)
y = np.linspace(-2, 2, 40)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
U = -Y
V = X

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.streamplot(X, Y, U, V, density=1.2)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `streamplot()` is better when the field is dense. It emphasizes flow over local vectors.
entries.common_bug: Feeding irregular grids that are not compatible with streamplot expectations.

entries.title: Create a 2D histogram
entries.problem: Show density over two numeric variables.
entries.trigger: Scatter is too noisy and you need aggregated counts.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=5000)
y = x * 0.4 + rng.normal(size=5000)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
h = ax.hist2d(x, y, bins=40, cmap="magma")
fig.colorbar(h[3], ax=ax)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use `hist2d()` for dense bivariate data. It is useful when count density matters more than individual points.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that `hist2d()` returns multiple objects, not just the image.

entries.title: Set title and labels
entries.problem: Add semantic context to a plot.
entries.trigger: You need axis labels and a title before publication.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
ax.set_title("Trend")
ax.set_xlabel("Time")
ax.set_ylabel("Value")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Set labels on the Axes, not globally. Titles and labels should be short and specific.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting units in axis labels.

entries.title: Set axis limits
entries.problem: Control visible data range.
entries.trigger: Autoscaling shows too much or too little data.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
ax.set_xlim(0, 4)
ax.set_ylim(0, 10)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use explicit limits for consistent comparisons across figures. Limits also help focus on a region of interest.
entries.common_bug: Setting limits before all data is added and then being surprised by autoscale behavior.

entries.title: Customize ticks and tick labels
entries.problem: Show exactly the tick positions and names you need.
entries.trigger: Default tick placement is not suitable for the story.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 5])
ax.set_xticks([1, 2, 3], ["one", "two", "three"])
ax.set_yticks([2, 4, 6])
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use `set_xticks()` and `set_yticks()` for direct control. Pair them with readable labels.
entries.common_bug: Calling `set_xticklabels()` without first fixing tick locations.

entries.title: Rotate tick labels
entries.problem: Prevent tick label overlap.
entries.trigger: Category names or dates are long.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(["Category A", "Category B", "Category C"], [3, 5, 2])
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=30)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Rotation is the quickest fix for crowded x-axis labels. Use it with layout management.
entries.common_bug: Rotating labels but not adjusting figure size or layout.

entries.title: Set axis scale
entries.problem: Use logarithmic or other non-linear scaling.
entries.trigger: Your data spans multiple orders of magnitude.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.logspace(0, 3, 100)
y = x**2

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, y)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use scale changes for multiplicative data. Log scales are common in science and engineering plots.
entries.common_bug: Applying log scale to data containing zeros or negatives.

entries.title: Add grid lines
entries.problem: Improve value reading from the plot.
entries.trigger: You need reference lines for estimation.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
ax.grid(True, which="major", axis="both", linestyle="--", alpha=0.4)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Grid lines should be subtle, not dominant. Use them to support reading rather than decorate.
entries.common_bug: Making grid lines darker than the data.

entries.title: Set aspect ratio
entries.problem: Preserve geometry or equal scaling.
entries.trigger: Shapes, distances, or slopes must be visually accurate.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1])
ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `equal` is common for maps, circles, and geometry plots. Aspect control prevents distortion.
entries.common_bug: Using default aspect for shapes that need equal units.

entries.title: Add a secondary y-axis
entries.problem: Show a second scale derived from the primary y-axis.
entries.trigger: You need a transformed companion axis on the right.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
ax.plot(x, x**2)
secax = ax.secondary_yaxis("right", functions=(lambda y: y / 2, lambda y: y * 2))
secax.set_ylabel("Half scale")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use `secondary_yaxis()` for mathematically related scales. Keep the transform simple and invertible.
entries.common_bug: Using a secondary axis for unrelated units.

entries.title: Add twin y-axis
entries.problem: Overlay a second series with a different y-scale.
entries.trigger: Two quantities share x but have different units.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots()
ax2 = ax1.twinx()

ax1.plot(x, np.sin(x), color="tab:blue", label="sin")
ax2.plot(x, 100 * np.cos(x), color="tab:orange", label="100 cos")
ax1.set_ylabel("sin")
ax2.set_ylabel("100 cos")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `twinx()` creates a second y-axis sharing x. Use it when dual units are truly necessary.
entries.common_bug: Overloading one plot with too many unrelated scales.

entries.title: Add twin x-axis
entries.problem: Overlay a second x-scale at the top.
entries.trigger: You need paired horizontal units or transformed coordinates.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots()
ax2 = ax1.twiny()

ax1.plot(x, np.sin(x))
ax1.set_xlabel("Primary x")
ax2.set_xlabel("Secondary x")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `twiny()` shares y while adding a second x axis. It is less common than `twinx()`.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that the top axis has its own tick setup.

entries.title: Add a legend
entries.problem: Identify plotted series automatically or explicitly.
entries.trigger: More than one artist needs a label.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0, 5, 50)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, x, label="linear")
ax.plot(x, x**2, label="quadratic")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Legends use artist labels by default. Label the artists at creation time whenever possible.
entries.common_bug: Calling `legend()` before assigning any labels.

entries.title: Place a figure legend
entries.problem: Create one legend for multiple axes.
entries.trigger: A multi-panel figure shares the same series labels.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0, 5, 50)
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3), layout="constrained")
l1, = axs[0].plot(x, x, label="linear")
l2, = axs[1].plot(x, x**2, label="quadratic")
fig.legend(handles=[l1, l2], loc="outside upper right")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `fig.legend()` is useful for shared legends across panels. Use `constrained_layout` for outside placement.
entries.common_bug: Putting a separate legend in every subplot when one shared legend is enough.

entries.title: Create a custom legend
entries.problem: Build a legend from proxy artists.
entries.trigger: The plotted object does not generate the legend you want.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9], color="tab:blue")

handles = [
    Line2D([0], [0], color="tab:blue", lw=2, label="Measured"),
    Line2D([0], [0], color="tab:orange", lw=2, linestyle="--", label="Target"),
]
ax.legend(handles=handles)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Proxy artists are useful when the real plot elements are too complex. Build the legend you need, not the one Matplotlib guesses.
entries.common_bug: Using actual data objects when a proxy artist would be simpler.

entries.title: Add text to an Axes
entries.problem: Place free text at a specific data coordinate.
entries.trigger: You need a simple label on the plot.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
ax.text(2, 5, "Peak region", fontsize=10)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `text()` is for labels and short annotations. Choose coordinates carefully.
entries.common_bug: Confusing data coordinates with axes coordinates.

entries.title: Annotate a point with an arrow
entries.problem: Call out a specific data point.
entries.trigger: You need a label connected to a plotted value.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
ax.annotate("max", xy=(3, 9), xytext=(2.2, 8),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `annotate()` is the standard callout API. It handles arrows and offset labels together.
entries.common_bug: Placing annotation text directly on top of the data point.

entries.title: Render mathematical expressions
entries.problem: Include formula-like text in labels or annotations.
entries.trigger: You need TeX-style math in a figure.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9], label=r"$y = x2$")
ax.set_title(r"Model: $f(x)$")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use raw strings for math text. Math rendering works in titles, labels, and annotations.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting raw string prefixes and escaping backslashes incorrectly.

entries.title: Use LaTeX rendering
entries.problem: Render full LaTeX text in a figure.
entries.trigger: You need document-quality math or serif typography.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

mpl.rcParams["text.usetex"] = False

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.set_title(r"Inline math: $\alpha + \beta$")
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Native mathtext is usually enough and avoids external LaTeX dependencies. Enable full LaTeX only when your environment supports it.
entries.common_bug: Turning on `text.usetex` in environments without a LaTeX installation.

entries.title: Use tight layout
entries.problem: Reduce overlapping labels automatically.
entries.trigger: Labels, titles, or tick labels crowd the figure edges.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 1)
axs[0].set_title("Top panel")
axs[1].set_xlabel("X axis")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `tight_layout()` is a quick spacing fix. It works well for many simple figures.
entries.common_bug: Using it when a more complex layout engine is needed.

entries.title: Use constrained layout
entries.problem: Let Matplotlib manage figure spacing robustly.
entries.trigger: You want automatic spacing for multi-panel figures.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, layout="constrained")
for ax in axs.ravel():
    ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `layout="constrained"` is the modern default choice for many figures. It handles titles, labels, and colorbars well.
entries.common_bug: Combining constrained layout with manual spacing tweaks that fight the engine.

entries.title: Adjust subplot spacing manually
entries.problem: Fine-tune panel gaps yourself.
entries.trigger: The default spacing is close, but not perfect.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6, 4))
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.3, hspace=0.4, left=0.08, right=0.98, top=0.92)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `subplots_adjust()` is the manual spacing tool. Use it when automated layout is not enough.
entries.common_bug: Overusing manual margins and breaking responsiveness.

entries.title: Share axes across subplots
entries.problem: Keep scales aligned across panels.
entries.trigger: You compare multiple plots on the same x or y scale.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(6, 4), layout="constrained")
axs[0].plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
axs[1].plot([1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 5])
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Shared axes help comparisons and reduce label clutter. Use them for small multiples.
entries.common_bug: Accidentally hiding needed tick labels on shared subplots.

entries.title: Add an inset Axes
entries.problem: Show a zoomed detail inside a main plot.
entries.trigger: You need a close-up view without a separate figure.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mpl_toolkits.axes_grid1.inset_locator import inset_axes

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 9, 16])

axins = inset_axes(ax, width="40%", height="40%", loc="upper left")
axins.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Insets are useful for detail views and zoom windows. Keep inset content simple.
entries.common_bug: Making the inset too large and obscuring the main plot.

entries.title: Apply a style sheet
entries.problem: Switch the global visual theme.
entries.trigger: You need a consistent publication or house style.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.style.use("seaborn-v0_8-whitegrid")
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Styles are the fastest way to change defaults. Apply them before creating figures.
entries.common_bug: Mixing multiple style changes without knowing which one wins.

entries.title: Update rcParams
entries.problem: Set defaults for the whole session or script.
entries.trigger: You want repeatable styling across many plots.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

mpl.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 150,
    "axes.grid": True,
    "lines.linewidth": 2,
})

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `rcParams` are session-wide defaults. Set only the parameters you need.
entries.common_bug: Mutating global defaults in shared notebook state and affecting later plots.

entries.title: Use a temporary style context
entries.problem: Apply styling only inside a block.
entries.trigger: You want local changes without global side effects.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

with plt.style.context("ggplot"):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
    plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Context managers keep style changes contained. This is safer in reusable code.
entries.common_bug: Leaving global style changes active after the plot is created.

entries.title: Select line and marker styles
entries.problem: Tune the appearance of a plotted series.
entries.trigger: You need publication-friendly line emphasis.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9], color="tab:blue", linestyle="--", marker="o", linewidth=2, alpha=0.8)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Line style, marker, width, color, and alpha cover most appearance needs. Keep styling consistent across series.
entries.common_bug: Overusing markers on dense line charts.

entries.title: Use a property cycler
entries.problem: Cycle through a custom set of colors or styles.
entries.trigger: You have multiple series and want consistent styling.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from cycler import cycler

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.set_prop_cycle(cycler(color=["#4C78A8", "#F58518", "#54A24B"]))
for i in range(3):
    ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [j + i for j in [1, 4, 9]])
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Property cycling keeps multi-series plots visually organized. It is especially useful for repeated dashboards.
entries.common_bug: Manually setting every series color and losing consistency.

entries.title: Use built-in colormaps
entries.problem: Choose a standard color gradient.
entries.trigger: You need a named colormap for an image or contour plot.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

data = np.random.default_rng(0).random((20, 20))
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
im = ax.imshow(data, cmap="viridis")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use named built-in colormaps for portability and clarity. Prefer perceptually uniform maps for scalar data.
entries.common_bug: Using rainbow-style maps for data that needs ordered perception.

entries.title: Normalize a colormap
entries.problem: Map values into a specific color scaling range.
entries.trigger: You need linear, logarithmic, or centered color mapping.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.colors import Normalize

data = np.linspace(0, 100, 100).reshape(10, 10)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
im = ax.imshow(data, cmap="viridis", norm=Normalize(vmin=0, vmax=100))
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Normalization controls how data maps into colors. Use it explicitly when figures must be comparable.
entries.common_bug: Comparing two heatmaps with different implicit scaling.

entries.title: Use discrete color bins
entries.problem: Show binned or categorical scalar levels.
entries.trigger: Continuous shading is too detailed for the message.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.colors import BoundaryNorm

data = np.random.default_rng(0).random((20, 20)) * 4
bounds = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
norm = BoundaryNorm(bounds, ncolors=256)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
im = ax.imshow(data, cmap="viridis", norm=norm)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, boundaries=bounds)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Discrete bins make thresholds explicit. They are useful for regimes or severity levels.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to align the colorbar boundaries with the bin edges.

entries.title: Plot datetime values
entries.problem: Render time-series with actual dates.
entries.trigger: Your x-axis uses Python datetime objects.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

dates = [datetime(2026, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=i) for i in range(10)]
values = [i * i for i in range(10)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(dates, values)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b %d"))
fig.autofmt_xdate()
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Matplotlib handles datetime objects directly. Formatters and locators control readability.
entries.common_bug: Letting date labels overlap on dense time axes.

entries.title: Control date locators
entries.problem: Choose date tick spacing explicitly.
entries.trigger: Default date ticks are too sparse or too dense.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

dates = [datetime(2026, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=i) for i in range(90)]
values = [i % 10 for i in range(90)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(dates, values)
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator())
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b"))
fig.autofmt_xdate()
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Locators choose tick positions and formatters choose labels. Use both together for clean time axes.
entries.common_bug: Setting only the formatter and leaving poor tick spacing in place.

entries.title: Use a broken-axis workflow
entries.problem: Show disjoint ranges without wasting space.
entries.trigger: One outlier range compresses the important region.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True, figsize=(6, 4),
                               gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1, 2]}, layout="constrained")
x = np.arange(10)
y = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55])

ax1.plot(x, y)
ax2.plot(x, y)
ax1.set_ylim(48, 56)
ax2.set_ylim(0, 5)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: A broken-axis effect is usually built from stacked axes. Keep the break visually obvious to avoid misreading.
entries.common_bug: Using a broken axis without marking the discontinuity.

entries.title: Add a colorbar
entries.problem: Interpret scalar color mapping.
entries.trigger: You use `imshow`, `contourf`, `pcolormesh`, or similar.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

data = np.random.default_rng(0).random((20, 20))
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
im = ax.imshow(data, cmap="viridis")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="Intensity")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Colorbars should be attached to the mappable object. Label the scale when the values matter.
entries.common_bug: Creating a colorbar without passing the actual image or contour object.

entries.title: Add an inset indicator
entries.problem: Mark the zoomed region on the parent plot.
entries.trigger: You have an inset and need to show where it came from.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mpl_toolkits.axes_grid1.inset_locator import inset_axes, mark_inset

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 9, 16])

axins = inset_axes(ax, width="40%", height="40%", loc="upper left")
axins.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
mark_inset(ax, axins, loc1=2, loc2=4)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Indicators connect inset and source region. They are common in publication figures.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to set the inset limits before drawing the connector.

entries.title: Save as PNG
entries.problem: Export a raster figure for reports or slides.
entries.trigger: You need a pixel-based image file.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4), dpi=150)
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
fig.savefig("figure.png", dpi=300)
entries.minimal_notes: PNG is the common default for raster export. Set `dpi` explicitly for predictable output quality.
entries.common_bug: Saving with low DPI and getting blurry text.

entries.title: Save as SVG
entries.problem: Export scalable vector graphics for editing or web.
entries.trigger: You need crisp line art at any zoom level.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
fig.savefig("figure.svg")
entries.minimal_notes: SVG is useful for web and vector editors. It preserves scalable text and paths.
entries.common_bug: Expecting SVG to behave like a raster image in every viewer.

entries.title: Save as PDF
entries.problem: Export a vector figure for papers and print.
entries.trigger: You need publication-ready document output.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
fig.savefig("figure.pdf")
entries.minimal_notes: PDF is the standard vector export for many journals. It is often the safest archival format.
entries.common_bug: Rasterizing the whole figure accidentally when vector output is desired.

entries.title: Save with transparent background
entries.problem: Place a figure over another background.
entries.trigger: You need a logo, overlay, or web asset.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
fig.savefig("figure.png", transparent=True)
entries.minimal_notes: Transparency is useful for overlays and slides. Check that text remains readable on the target background.
entries.common_bug: Exporting transparent figures with low-contrast labels.

entries.title: Save with tight bounding box
entries.problem: Trim extra whitespace around the figure.
entries.trigger: You need compact export output.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
fig.savefig("figure.png", bbox_inches="tight")
entries.minimal_notes: `bbox_inches="tight"` is common for papers and reports. It trims surrounding whitespace.
entries.common_bug: Cropping away annotation text placed near the edges.

entries.title: Add metadata when saving
entries.problem: Embed author or title information in output files.
entries.trigger: You need tracked or publication metadata.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])
fig.savefig("figure.pdf", metadata={"Title": "Example Figure", "Author": "AENS"})
entries.minimal_notes: Metadata is supported on several output formats. Use it for document management and provenance.
entries.common_bug: Assuming every format stores the same metadata keys.

entries.title: Rasterize dense artists in vector output
entries.problem: Keep vector exports small and fast.
entries.trigger: Your figure has huge scatter or heatmap layers.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=200000)
y = rng.normal(size=200000)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sc = ax.scatter(x, y, s=1, rasterized=True)
fig.savefig("dense.pdf")
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Rasterization is useful inside PDF or SVG when a layer is too dense. Keep text and axes vector while rasterizing only heavy artists.
entries.common_bug: Rasterizing the entire figure instead of only the dense layer.

entries.title: Simplify paths for large plots
entries.problem: Reduce draw cost for long line series.
entries.trigger: You plot very dense polylines.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

mpl.rcParams["path.simplify"] = True
mpl.rcParams["path.simplify_threshold"] = 0.5

x = np.linspace(0, 1000, 200000)
y = np.sin(x)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, y)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Path simplification can speed up rendering for dense lines. Keep the threshold conservative.
entries.common_bug: Simplifying too aggressively and altering important detail.

entries.title: Reuse figures in loops
entries.problem: Generate many similar plots efficiently.
entries.trigger: You are batch-rendering charts.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for i in range(3):
    ax.clear()
    ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [j + i for j in [1, 4, 9]])
    fig.canvas.draw()
entries.minimal_notes: Reusing the same figure can be faster than recreating it repeatedly. Clear the Axes between draws.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to clear the Axes and accumulating old lines.

entries.title: Use interactive callbacks efficiently
entries.problem: Update plots in response to user actions.
entries.trigger: You need live interaction or GUI-driven plots.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
line, = ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1, 4, 9])

def on_click(event):
    if event.inaxes == ax:
        line.set_ydata([1, 2, 3])
        fig.canvas.draw_idle()

fig.canvas.mpl_connect("button_press_event", on_click)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use `draw_idle()` for event-driven updates. Keep callback work small.
entries.common_bug: Doing heavy computation directly inside GUI event handlers.

entries.title: Create a FuncAnimation
entries.problem: Animate changing plot data over time.
entries.trigger: You need frame-by-frame updates from a function.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
import numpy as np

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)
line, = ax.plot(x, np.sin(x))

def update(frame):
    line.set_ydata(np.sin(x + frame / 10))
    return line,

ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=60, interval=30, blit=True)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `FuncAnimation` is the standard dynamic animation API. Return the modified artists for blitting.
entries.common_bug: Not retaining a reference to the animation object.

entries.title: Create an ArtistAnimation
entries.problem: Animate a sequence of prebuilt frames.
entries.trigger: Your frames already exist as artists.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import ArtistAnimation

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
frames = []
for i in range(3):
    art = ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [1 + i, 4 + i, 9 + i], color="tab:blue")
    frames.append(art)

ani = ArtistAnimation(fig, frames, interval=300, blit=True)
plt.show()
entries.minimal_notes: `ArtistAnimation` is suitable when frames are already available. It is less flexible than `FuncAnimation`.
entries.common_bug: Generating too many artists and using excessive memory.

entries.title: Save an animation
entries.problem: Export an animation to a file.
entries.trigger: You need MP4 or GIF output from a Matplotlib animation.
entries.snippet:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
import numpy as np

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)
line, = ax.plot(x, np.sin(x))

def update(frame):
    line.set_ydata(np.sin(x + frame / 10))
    return line,

ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=30, interval=30, blit=True)
ani.save("anim.gif", writer="pillow", fps=20)
entries.minimal_notes: Choose the writer based on your environment. Saving animation usually requires an installed encoder or Pillow.
entries.common_bug: Trying to save without a supported writer installed.

quick_references.title: Common Errors & Troubleshooting
rows: Figure too small or layout not managed.
Add labels when creating the artists.
Limits set too early or too narrowly.
Set limits after plotting and verify units.
Many figures left open in loops.
Low DPI or wrong export size.
Increase `dpi` and figure size before saving.
Unsupported GUI backend or missing display.
Use a suitable backend for the environment.

quick_references.title: Performance Checklist
rows: Prefer `Axes` methods over repeated stateful pyplot calls.
Close figures after saving in batch jobs.
Rasterize dense scatter, image, or contour layers in vector exports.
Simplify long line paths when plots are visually unchanged.
Reuse a figure in loops when generating many similar charts.
Use a suitable backend for interactive sessions and scripts.
Keep callbacks lightweight in interactive plots.
Prefer smaller datasets or downsample before plotting when possible.

quick_references.title: Production Deployment Checklist
rows: Use the OO API by default.
Set explicit figure size and DPI for final output.
Use readable labels, units, and titles.
Keep layouts consistent with `constrained_layout` or a controlled alternative.
Verify exports in the target format before release.
Save vector formats for publication when appropriate.
Avoid duplicate legends, ambiguous scales, and overdecorated plots.
Close figures in automation and notebooks when done.
Keep snippets stable, runnable, and import complete.

quick_references.title: Legend locations
rows: Default when plot area is free.
Good when upper area is dense.
